title: LEV extraction loses capture weeks after its 14-month test and nobody notices until HSE visits
problem: Welding-fume or wood-dust LEV loses capture: a filter blinds, a fan belt slips or a damper is left shut, often weeks after the annual thorough examination and test (TExT). Workers breathe fume or dust for months. The HSE inspector finds it and issues an improvement notice plus Fee for Intervention (~£170/h). Occupational asthma or COPD claims run ~£10k–£100k+.
who_suffers: Welders, joiners and grinders on the shop floor; the H&S lead who signs the COSHH assessment
buyer: Health & Safety Manager or Works/Engineering Manager at an SME fabricator or joinery
industry: UK metal fabrication, welding shops and joinery/woodworking manufacturers
current_workaround: Contractor TExT every 14 months (~£300–£1,000 per system). Operators are meant to check the hood manometer/airflow indicator weekly and write it in a paper LEV logbook, but this is often skipped or pencil-whipped.
sensor_concept: Differential-pressure sensor (Sensirion SDP-class) tapped into the hood plenum/duct, plus a current clamp on the fan motor. LoRaWAN or NB-IoT, battery. Alerts when static pressure leaves the commissioned band, and auto-generates the weekly check record and LEV logbook PDF for the TExT contractor and the HSE.
notes: c4 strong (COSHH reg 9, HSG258, HSE welding-fume enforcement push); c2 weekly checks; c6 LEV test contractors already visit every site annually and could resell; cheap DP sensor for c8.

title: Cooling-tower biocide drum runs dry between monthly water-treatment visits
problem: On a factory cooling tower or evaporative condenser, the biocide/inhibitor day tank empties or the dosing pump airlocks. The tower runs undosed for ~2–4 weeks until the contractor's monthly visit. High TVC or Legionella counts follow and force a chlorination/clean (~£1–3k each). In the worst case there is an outbreak, and HSE cooling-tower prosecutions bring fines of £100k–£1m+.
who_suffers: Site engineers, nearby public and workforce; the duty holder named in the L8 written scheme
buyer: Site Engineering/Facilities Manager (duty holder), or the water-treatment contractor's account manager as a bundled service
industry: Manufacturing and process sites with notifiable cooling towers/evaporative condensers (UK NCTEC Regs 1992)
current_workaround: Weekly on-site checks under L8/HSG274 Part 1 (dosing, bleed, conductivity), weekly dip slides and monthly contractor service visits with paper or contractor-portal logs
sensor_concept: Ultrasonic/ToF level (or load cell) on each chemical day tank, a vibration/current sensor proving the dosing pump strokes, and a sump water temperature probe. NB-IoT/LTE-M, mains or battery. Alerts the contractor and site when dosing stops, and auto-fills the weekly HSG274 check record.
notes: c4 likely 9–10 (L8 ACOP, HSG274, notification regs, many HSE prosecutions); c6 water-treatment contractors visit monthly and sell dosing kit; c2 weekly mandated checks.

title: CNC coolant (metalworking fluid) sumps drift out of spec because weekly COSHH checks are skipped
problem: HSE MW5 guidance expects weekly concentration (refractometer), pH and dip-slide bacteria checks on every water-mix MWF sump. Busy machine shops skip them. Fluid goes rancid, causing dermatitis and occupational asthma/hypersensitivity pneumonitis (the Powertrain outbreak hit ~100 workers), dump-and-recharge (~£500–£2k per machine) and poor tool life. Inspectors ask to see the records.
who_suffers: CNC operators (skin and lungs); production managers facing downtime
buyer: Production/Operations Manager or H&S Manager at a precision engineering or automotive supplier
industry: UK precision engineering / CNC machine shops using water-mix metalworking fluids
current_workaround: Manual weekly refractometer, pH strip and dip-slide incubator by a setter, logged on paper; fluid supplier technicians do periodic sump surveys
sensor_concept: In-sump probe for conductivity, temperature and liquid level (concentration proxy and top-up need), with optional ISFET pH. LoRaWAN/NB-IoT. Weekly per-machine COSHH record and drift alerts; tramp-oil level flagged from the level/temperature signature.
notes: c2 weekly mandated task; c4 COSHH + HSE MW5; c6 MWF suppliers (Fuchs, Quaker Houghton, Castrol, Master Fluid Solutions) run fluid-management site visits; c8 risk: probe fouling/calibration.

title: Emergency safety showers and eyewashes: unproven weekly flush, unseen real activations
problem: Chemical-handling plants should flush emergency showers and eyewashes weekly (ANSI Z358.1 in the US; BS EN 15154 and L8 dead-leg Legionella advice in the UK). Flushes are missed, so stagnant water reaches an injured eye. A real activation in a remote corner at night goes unseen while a splashed worker is alone. OSHA serious citations run ~$16k each (US), and UK RIDDOR investigations follow.
who_suffers: Operators handling acids/caustics; EHS lead
buyer: EHS Manager at a chemical, plating or water-treatment-chemicals plant
industry: Chemical processing, electroplating/surface treatment and battery/acid handling plants
current_workaround: Weekly manual flush with a paper tag on each unit; annual ANSI/EN inspection by a supplier
sensor_concept: Clamp-on pipe temperature differential plus a vibration/flow sensor on the shower supply detects every activation and its duration. LoRaWAN/NB-IoT, 5-year battery. Weekly flush log per unit, instant alert on unscheduled activation (possible injury), and a Legionella stagnation flag.
notes: c2 weekly task; c4 ANSI Z358.1/OSHA (US) and L8 (UK); c6 safety-shower suppliers and water-hygiene contractors already service units; c8 very cheap.

title: Steam boiler daily/weekly water-level control tests not evidenced for the insurer's engineer
problem: Under PSSR and SAFed BG01, unattended-operation steam boilers need daily/weekly blowdown and low-water alarm tests recorded in a log. At the annual insurance inspection, missing or fabricated logs lead to a requirement or a boiler taken out of service. A low-water-cutoff failure that goes unnoticed can wreck the boiler (~£20k–£100k+) and halt production.
who_suffers: Boiler attendants and maintenance team; production halted when the boiler is down
buyer: Maintenance/Engineering Manager at a food, textile, chemical or brewing plant
industry: Industrial plants running shell steam boilers under PSSR 2000 written schemes
current_workaround: Daily attendance and paper boiler log, weekly evaporation test, annual examination by insurer engineer surveyors (HSB, Allianz, Zurich Engineering)
sensor_concept: Surface-temperature clamps on the blowdown lines plus burner-current and pressure monitoring infer each blowdown/test event and burner lockout. NB-IoT. Auto-generated BG01-style log, missed-test alerts and a downloadable record for the engineer surveyor.
notes: c4 PSSR + BG01 and insurer inspection; c2 daily/weekly test; c6 engineering-insurer surveyors and boiler service firms visit; value is record-keeping (c9).

title: Machine guard interlocks defeated on the shop floor with no record until an amputation
problem: Operators tape over or bypass interlock switches, or use spare actuator keys, to speed up jams and setting. It happens daily on some machines and nobody knows until an amputation. HSE prosecutions under PUWER reg 11 routinely bring fines of ~£100k–£1m+.
who_suffers: Machine operators; production supervisors; directors personally exposed
buyer: Production Manager or H&S Manager at a packaging, plastics, print or metal-forming plant
industry: UK packaging, plastics, print and metal-pressing manufacturers
current_workaround: Periodic PUWER inspections and supervisor walk-rounds; interlock function tests on PM schedules; no way to see bypass behaviour between visits
sensor_concept: Independent reed/magnet sensor on the guard door plus a current clamp on the main drive motor. It logs every instance of machine running while the guard is open and sends a daily bypass report. LoRaWAN, battery. A non-safety audit layer, so no PL/SIL certification.
notes: c1/c10 strong (frequent HSE prosecutions with big fines); c2 daily events; c6 PUWER/machinery-safety consultants and engineering insurers visit; must be framed as audit, not a safety function.

title: Oil-tank and IBC bunds fill with rainwater so the next leak overtops into the drain
problem: External bunds round diesel, hydraulic oil and chemical tanks or IBC spill pallets fill with rainwater, losing their 110% capacity. When a tank or valve leaks, oil overtops into a surface-water drain. The result is Environment Agency enforcement or prosecution (fines ~£10k–£100k+) plus clean-up of ~£10k+.
who_suffers: Site manager, environmental lead; neighbours/watercourse
buyer: Environmental/Facilities Manager at a manufacturing site
industry: UK manufacturing and industrial sites storing >200 L oil above ground (Control of Pollution (Oil Storage) (England) Regs 2001)
current_workaround: Weekly visual bund inspection on a checklist (often skipped), manual pumping-out of rainwater, annual tank inspection by OFTEC/tank contractor
sensor_concept: ToF/ultrasonic level in the bund plus a capacitive oil/water discrimination probe at the sump. NB-IoT, battery. Alerts when bund liquid reaches X% (rainwater, so pump out) or when oil is detected (leak). Auto weekly inspection log for EA/insurer.
notes: c4 named regulation + EA enforcement; c6 oil distributors, tank installers and waste-oil collectors visit; c8 cheap; must differentiate from domestic heating-oil tank monitors.

title: Engineered-stone worktop fabricators cutting quartz with the water suppression off
problem: Quartz/engineered stone is up to ~90% crystalline silica. Water suppression on bridge saws and hand tools is often turned off, blocked or frozen in winter to avoid mess. HSE ran a targeted engineered-stone inspection campaign (2023–24) issuing notices, and silicosis claims run ~£k–£100k+, with young workers diagnosed in other countries (Australia banned the material).
who_suffers: Stone cutters and polishers (silicosis); small workshop owners
buyer: Owner/Workshop Manager of a kitchen-worktop fabrication business
industry: UK kitchen worktop / engineered-stone fabrication workshops
current_workaround: Supervisor observation, RPE face-fit tests, periodic LEV tests; no record of whether wet-cutting was actually used during each cut
sensor_concept: Inline flow switch/sensor on each tool's water feed plus a current clamp on the tool or saw. LoRaWAN or LTE-M. Logs the % of cutting time with water flowing, alerts when a tool runs dry, and gives a monthly COSHH control-measure report.
notes: c4 HSE campaign + COSHH; c10 high public profile (silicosis, Australian ban); c6 stone machinery dealers and RPE fit-testers visit; c5 small firms is a risk.

title: Foundry fettling and grinding HAV exposure estimated on paper, then a HAVS claim lands
problem: Hand-arm vibration exposure in fettling shops is estimated from tool datasheets × guessed trigger times. Workers exceed the exposure action/limit values, and RIDDOR-reportable HAVS follows. HSE prosecutions bring fines of ~£100k–£800k, and civil HAVS claims run ~£k–£30k each.
who_suffers: Fettlers and grinders; H&S manager
buyer: H&S Manager at a foundry, steel fabricator or castings finisher
industry: UK foundries, castings fettling and heavy fabrication grinding shops
current_workaround: Paper trigger-time estimates, job rotation rotas, annual health surveillance questionnaires; some use Reactec HAVwear (premium wearable)
sensor_concept: Tool-mounted accelerometer plus a current sensor logging actual trigger time and vibration magnitude per tool. A BLE operator tag links the tool to a person, with a cellular gateway in the shop. Daily exposure points per worker against the EAV/ELV and a records export for health surveillance.
notes: c4 Control of Vibration at Work Regs + frequent HSE enforcement; c2 daily exposure; c7 Reactec proves WTP but is premium; c6 tool distributors/hire firms.

title: Trade-effluent pH/flow consent breaches discovered by the water company's sampler, not the factory
problem: A factory's trade-effluent consent sets pH (~6–10), flow and strength limits. A neutralisation dosing failure sends acid or caustic to sewer overnight, and the water company's spot sample catches it. Consequences are prosecution (fines ~£k–£100k+), Mogden surcharge uplifts and consent review.
who_suffers: Site environmental lead; production (forced shutdowns)
buyer: Environmental/Utilities Manager at a metal-finishing, drinks or chemical plant
industry: UK manufacturing sites discharging trade effluent under Water Industry Act consents
current_workaround: Daily manual pH checks with a handheld meter at the final chamber, paper log; legacy pH controller with local display only
sensor_concept: pH plus conductivity and temperature probe at the final discharge chamber, and a pulse/flow reader on the discharge meter. NB-IoT. Breach alerts, a continuous consent-compliance log and a monthly report. Includes a probe-swap/recalibration service as the consumable.
notes: c4 named consent + water-company prosecutions; c9 recalibration/probe consumable; c8 risk: pH probe drift and maintenance (scores ~5–6).

title: Warehouse sprinkler pump-house weekly test log faked or skipped, so the insurer challenges the claim
problem: LPC Rules/TB203 and BS EN 12845 require a weekly sprinkler pump start test (diesel run ≥30 min), fuel/oil checks and valve-pressure readings, all logged. On lightly staffed DCs the weekly test is skipped, frost hits the pump house, or the diesel battery is flat. An impaired system found after a fire puts a £m warehouse loss and insurer conditions precedent in play.
who_suffers: DC site/facilities team; insurer; tenants' stock
buyer: Site Facilities Manager or Property Manager of a distribution centre
industry: UK sprinklered distribution centres and big-box warehouses (insurer LPC-rule installations)
current_workaround: Weekly manual test by a site engineer with a paper/LPC logbook, quarterly sprinkler contractor service, annual insurer risk survey
sensor_concept: Pressure transducers on the installation/trunk main, vibration/current detection of jockey and main pump runs, diesel tank level, pump-house temperature and starter battery voltage. NB-IoT/LTE-M. Auto-builds the TB203 weekly test record, alerts on missed test, frost or low fuel, and shares with sprinkler contractor and insurer.
notes: c4 9–10 (insurer rules, conditions precedent); c2 weekly task; c6 sprinkler maintenance contractors and insurer risk engineers already visit; c1 needs per-incident £ beyond rare fires.

title: Pallet racking uprights hit several times a week with no report until the weekly inspection
problem: In busy DCs, reach trucks clip racking uprights several times a week and drivers don't report it. SEMA's red-risk damage then sits loaded until the weekly visual or annual SARI inspection. Upright repair costs ~£150–£500. Collapses cost ~£100k+ in stock and racking, and bring HSE action.
who_suffers: Warehouse operatives under racking; racking safety (PRRS) lead
buyer: Warehouse/Operations Manager or the Person Responsible for Racking Safety (PRRS)
industry: UK 3PL and retail distribution warehouses with adjustable pallet racking
current_workaround: Weekly PRRS visual walk-round with paper checklist, annual SEMA/SARI expert inspection (~£k), damage-reporting culture campaigns
sensor_concept: Accelerometer/tilt tag on upright protectors or uprights (LoRaWAN, 5-year battery) logs impact severity, time and bay. Alerts the PRRS to inspect immediately, cross-matches with forklift shift, and auto-prioritises the weekly inspection route.
notes: c2 multiple impacts/week; c4 SEMA guidance, PUWER, HSG76; c6 SARI inspectors and racking installers visit; c7 A-SAFE RackEye proves market but premium.

title: High-speed and sectional dock doors struck by forklifts weekly; culprit and timing unknown
problem: Busy DCs suffer forklift and trailer strikes on high-speed and sectional doors roughly weekly. Each repair costs ~£1–5k plus callout. The bay is out of service, letting in heat or cold (chilled docks), and nobody knows who hit it or when. Door maintainers argue over whether it was wear or damage.
who_suffers: Shift managers, door engineers, transport schedulers
buyer: Warehouse Engineering/Facilities Manager
industry: UK distribution centres with multiple dock doors and internal high-speed doors
current_workaround: Reactive callouts to door maintenance contractor; 6-monthly planned maintenance (DHF TS011/BS EN 12453 requirements for powered doors); CCTV trawling
sensor_concept: Accelerometer on the door bottom rail/curtain plus a reed cycle counter. LoRaWAN. Impact alerts with timestamp (for CCTV and shift match), cycle counts for usage-based servicing, and a damage log shared with the door contractor.
notes: c2 weekly damage; c6 industrial-door maintenance firms visit 2×/yr and would resell for more callouts; c3 paid repairs/callouts; c4 weaker (powered door maintenance records).

title: Forklift traction batteries under-watered and killed early; battery contract disputes
problem: Flooded lead-acid forklift batteries need watering roughly weekly and correct charging. Shift teams forget or over-opportunity-charge, and a ~£3–8k battery dies years early. Rental and battery-service firms dispute who misused it.
who_suffers: Fleet/MHE coordinators; battery service provider
buyer: MHE/Fleet Manager at a 3PL, or the forklift dealer's service manager (as a value-add)
industry: UK warehouses running mixed electric counterbalance/reach fleets with flooded lead-acid batteries
current_workaround: Weekly manual watering rota, paper watering log, monthly battery-service visits with hydrometer checks
sensor_concept: Electrolyte level probe in a pilot cell, cell temperature, and a clamp CT on charge leads (charge/discharge cycles), BLE to a cellular gateway in the charging room. Watering-due alerts, abuse events (deep discharge, opportunity charging) and a battery-health report for the contract.
notes: c3 weekly labour + paid service; c6 forklift dealers/battery service firms visit monthly; c7 EnerSys Wi-iQ is incumbent on new batteries, gap is retrofit/mixed fleets.

title: Ambient medicines in a 3PL warehouse go over 25°C in a heatwave; MHRA GDP finding and quarantine
problem: MHRA Good Distribution Practice requires mapped, continuously monitored 15–25°C storage for medicines. In summer heatwaves high bays and mezzanines exceed 25°C. Stock is quarantined or destroyed (~£k–£100k per excursion), and MHRA inspection findings put the WDA(H) licence at risk.
who_suffers: Responsible Person (RP) under the WDA(H); 3PL quality team
buyer: Quality Manager / Responsible Person at a 3PL or pharma wholesaler
industry: UK 3PL and wholesale warehouses holding ambient medicines, supplements and OTC products under WDA(H)
current_workaround: Standalone USB data loggers downloaded weekly; annual summer/winter temperature mapping by consultants; manual daily min/max checks
sensor_concept: Multi-height LoRaWAN temperature/RH probes with UKAS-traceable calibration certificates and an alarm/audit trail. Gateway on cellular backhaul (no client IT). Excursion alerts, GDP-format reports, and recalibration-swap service as the recurring item.
notes: c4 MHRA GDP + inspection findings; c9 recalibration and records; c7 crowded (Vaisala, ELPRO) so the gap is SME 3PLs; c8 calibration cert pushes cost.

title: Dairy and grocery roll cages vanish at stores and scrap yards
problem: Dairies, bakeries and grocery distributors lose large numbers of roll cages and dollies (~£80–£150 each) every year. They are left at stores, used as storage, or stolen for scrap. Nobody can show which customer is holding them, so replacement and recharging disputes cost £k–£100k per year per fleet.
who_suffers: Transport/equipment pool managers; drivers chasing returns
buyer: Equipment Pool / Logistics Manager at a dairy, bakery or wholesale distributor
industry: UK dairy and bakery direct-to-store distribution and grocery wholesale
current_workaround: Manual cage counts at depot and stores, driver delivery notes, annual write-off and bulk repurchase
sensor_concept: Very low-cost LPWAN or BLE tags (target <£5–10) welded to each cage. Gateways at depots and on delivery vehicles log dwell by customer site. Monthly report of cages held per store for recharging, plus alerts for cages at scrap yards.
notes: c1 large aggregate losses; c2 continuous; c9 pool-management subscription; c8 risk: per-tag BOM must be very low; c6 roll-cage makers/pool operators.

title: Bonded warehouse 'unexplained loss' leaves the warehousekeeper paying the excise duty
problem: HMRC assesses excise duty on unexplained losses and deficiencies in bonded warehouses (Excise Notice 197). A missing pallet of spirits is ~£15–25k duty, and repeated losses threaten the approval. Night-time pilferage or mis-picks from the bonded cage are hard to evidence.
who_suffers: Warehousekeeper (approval holder); bond security staff
buyer: Bonded Warehouse Manager / Approved Warehousekeeper
industry: UK excise (bonded) warehouses holding wines, spirits and tobacco
current_workaround: Stock counts, CCTV, access control on main doors, HMRC-required stock records; manual cage-key logs
sensor_concept: Door contacts and PIR on the bonded cage and high-value aisles, plus LoRa tags on high-value pallets (movement/tilt). Cellular gateway. Out-of-hours movement alerts and an access/movement log as evidence for HMRC loss explanations.
notes: c1 large duty per loss; c4 HMRC Notice 197 conditions; c2 risk: incidents may be infrequent; c6 bond security installers/bond insurers.

title: Overnight charging of e-cargo bikes and e-scooters in last-mile hubs, with insurer lithium conditions
problem: Last-mile delivery hubs and e-bike distributors charge or store dozens of lithium packs overnight. Insurers increasingly impose conditions (RISCAuthority/FPA guidance: segregated charging, supervision, detection). A thermal-runaway fire can destroy the hub (~£100k–£m), and policies get loaded or declined.
who_suffers: Hub managers; landlords; neighbours
buyer: Operations/Facilities Manager at a last-mile courier hub or e-bike distributor
industry: UK last-mile parcel/food delivery hubs and e-bike/e-scooter wholesale warehouses
current_workaround: Charging timers, manual end-of-day checks, ordinary smoke detection (slow for Li-ion), insurer surveys
sensor_concept: Multi-point thermistor strip along charging racks, an off-gas VOC/H2 sensor (early electrolyte venting) and smart-plug current per charger bank. LTE-M. Early alerts to the keyholder, auto charger cut-off, and a charging log for the insurer.
notes: c4 insurer conditions emerging; c6 insurers/brokers; c2 risk: value mostly rare catastrophe (score ~5), mitigated by daily charging-compliance log.

title: Lorry-yard oil interceptors overfill with oil and silt between 6-monthly emptying
problem: HGV yards and fuelling points drain through oil separators. Oil-level alarms are missing or broken, the separator fills with oil and silt, and oil discharges to a watercourse. The Environment Agency prosecutes (fines ~£10k–£100k+) and emergency tanker clean-up costs ~£k.
who_suffers: Depot manager; environmental lead
buyer: Depot/Facilities Manager at a haulage or distribution depot
industry: UK haulage depots, distribution yards and fleet fuelling points with BS EN 858 separators
current_workaround: 6-monthly or annual tanker emptying contract, visual checks by lifting covers, legacy alarm panels often disconnected
sensor_concept: Capacitance/conductivity oil-layer thickness probe plus an ultrasonic silt/liquid level sensor in the separator. NB-IoT, battery. Alerts at 90% oil capacity or high silt, with emptying-due forecasts sent directly to the emptying contractor.
notes: c4 BS EN 858/PPG3 + EA enforcement; c6 drainage/tanker contractors (Lanes, Metro Rod etc.) visit; c9 ties to emptying service; overlaps with forecourts, so keep to depots.

title: Loading-bay trailer creep and drive-aways because older docks have no restraint record
problem: At older loading bays, a trailer creeps or is driven off while a forklift is inside, and the forklift falls between dock and trailer. HSE prosecutions bring fines of ~£50k–£500k. Vehicle restraints are fitted on new docks only; older bays rely on drivers handing in keys, which is unenforced and unrecorded.
who_suffers: Forklift drivers; transport office; HGV drivers
buyer: Warehouse/Transport Operations Manager
industry: UK DCs and manufacturers with older raised loading docks
current_workaround: Key-safe or 'keys on hook' procedure, traffic lights operated manually, wheel chocks, periodic HSE-style audits
sensor_concept: Trailer-present radar/ultrasonic sensor, dock-door open contact, leveller deployed and chock-in-place magnet. LoRaWAN. Alerts when the door is open with a trailer present but no chock or restraint, plus per-bay compliance log and daily report.
notes: c4 HSE HSG136 loading-bay guidance + prosecutions; c2 daily compliance events; c6 dock equipment service firms (Hörmann, Stertil, Thorworld) visit; c7 retrofit gap vs integrated restraints.

title: Prison hot-water monthly sentinel checks missed by the FM contractor; Legionella death
problem: HSG274 requires monthly temperature checks at sentinel outlets and calorifiers. In prisons, escort requirements and lockdowns mean checks are missed. At HMP Lincoln, a prisoner died of Legionnaires' disease and Amey was fined £600k (Dec 2024) for failing to carry out temperature checks on a wing.
who_suffers: Prisoners and staff; FM contractor's compliance team
buyer: FM Contract Compliance/Water Hygiene Manager at the prison FM provider (e.g. GFSL, Amey, Mitie) or private operator
industry: UK prisons (public and private) and YOIs
current_workaround: Monthly manual thermometer rounds by escorted FM engineers, paper or CAFM records, annual risk assessment by water-hygiene contractor
sensor_concept: Clip-on pipe thermistors at sentinel outlets, TMVs and calorifier flow/return in service ducts (not in-cell). LoRaWAN with a private gateway on site, since cellular may be blocked or jammed in prisons. Auto HSG274 monthly report and flushing/temperature failure alerts.
notes: c1/c4 10-grade evidence (HSE £600k fine, HSG274 monthly checks); c2 monthly task; c6 FM contractor is the buyer and on site daily; c8 risk: RF in thick-walled prisons, cellular denial.

title: Police custody cell checks and rousing not done to schedule, then a death in custody
problem: PACE Code C Annex H requires 30-minute (or 15-minute) checks and rousing for intoxicated detainees. IOPC investigations repeatedly find spyhole-only or late checks, with gross misconduct cases and inquest findings. Civil claims and investigations cost ~£k–£100k+ per death.
who_suffers: Detainees; custody sergeants and detention officers facing misconduct
buyer: Head of Criminal Justice / Chief Inspector Custody in a police force (or custody outsourcer)
industry: UK police custody suites (and court cells run by escort contractors)
current_workaround: Manual entries of checks on the custody record system, sometimes retrospective; CCTV review after incidents; vital-signs camera systems in some suites (Oxehealth)
sensor_concept: Reed switch on each cell door hatch/door and BLE badge for the detention officer, giving a timestamped visit log against the required check interval. Gateway with cellular backhaul, no force IT. Overdue-check alerts on a tablet and an exportable visit log for audits and IOPC.
notes: c4/c10 strong (PACE, IOPC findings); c2 checks every 30 min; c5/c6 risk: police procurement and IT security; c7 Oxehealth incumbent for vital signs.

title: Prisoner escort vans: cubicle temperature and time-in-cubicle not evidenced
problem: Prisoners travel for hours in sealed cellular cubicles. In heatwaves cubicles can exceed ~30°C, and HMIP/IMB reports criticise long journeys without breaks. Escort contractors face service-credit deductions, complaints and litigation, and they cannot evidence the conditions on a disputed journey.
who_suffers: Prisoners; escort custody officers; contract managers
buyer: PECS contract Fleet/Operations Manager at the escort contractor (e.g. GEOAmey, Serco)
industry: UK Prisoner Escort and Custody Services (PECS) cellular vehicles
current_workaround: Paper/handheld journey records, vehicle telematics for location only, A/C serviced by fleet maintainer
sensor_concept: Per-cubicle temperature sensors, door/occupancy contact and GPS on a cellular telematics hub. Live welfare alerts (temp > threshold, time in cubicle > X h) and an auto journey welfare log per prisoner movement.
notes: c4 contract KPIs + HMIP; c5 concentrated buyers (few contractors); c6 cellular-van converters/fleet telematics installers; c2 daily journeys.

title: Prison key set walks out of the gate in an officer's pocket, forcing a full re-lock
problem: When a staff member takes a key set home or a pouch goes missing, the prison must re-lock wings or the whole establishment. Reported costs include ~£441k (Wandsworth 2018), ~£500k (Warren Hill), ~£117k (Portland) and up to ~£1m (Northumberland). Private operators pay re-locks themselves.
who_suffers: Governor, security department; private prison operators
buyer: Head of Security / Director of a private prison (or HMPPS security group)
industry: UK prisons and secure hospitals using mechanical key suites
current_workaround: Key chains and pouches, tally/key-safe and Traka-type key cabinets, gate-lodge manual checks at shift end
sensor_concept: Tamper-resistant BLE beacon fused into each key chain or pouch. LoRaWAN/BLE receivers at gate lodges and staff exit alarm if a key set passes the exit, and a shift-end reconciliation shows keys not returned to the cabinet.
notes: c1 10-grade (official re-lock costs £100k–£500k+); c2 daily key issue/return routine; c4 HMPPS security policy; c7 Traka cabinets don't catch keys leaving.

title: Deliberate cell flooding cascades onto landings and puts cells out of use
problem: Prisoners block toilets and sinks and flood cells, in some establishments daily. Water cascades to cells and electrics below, cells go out of use, and FM repair callouts cost ~£k per incident. Nobody can tell which cell started it or isolate it quickly.
who_suffers: Landing officers; FM engineers; prisoners in cells below
buyer: FM contract manager or Head of Estates/Residential Governor
industry: UK local and Category B/C prisons
current_workaround: Officers spot water on landings, manual isolation valves in service ducts, timed flush controllers on some wings
sensor_concept: Pulse flow sensor on each cell's water feed in the service duct plus leak strips on landing ducts. LoRaWAN private gateway. Abnormal-flow alerts identify the cell, with optional solenoid auto-isolation, and the log supports adjudications and cost recovery.
notes: c2 frequent (daily/weekly); c3 FM repair callouts; c6 FM provider on site; c8 vandal-proof install in ducts; c4 weaker (no named rule).

title: Police property-store freezers holding DNA exhibits fail over a weekend
problem: Biological exhibits (swabs, clothing, sexual-assault kits) are stored frozen or chilled. A freezer failing over a weekend degrades them, so re-analysis is impossible, cases are lost, and inquiries cost ~£k–£100k. The Forensic Science Regulator's statutory Code requires controlled storage and continuity records, and HMICFRS has criticised property stores.
who_suffers: Investigators, CPS, victims; property store staff
buyer: Head of Property & Exhibits / Forensic Services Manager in a police force
industry: UK police property/exhibit stores and forensic submission units
current_workaround: Daily manual min/max thermometer checks logged on paper/spreadsheets, building BMS alarms that don't reach on-call staff
sensor_concept: Glycol-buffered probe temperature, door contact and power sensor per freezer/fridge, with a cellular gateway (no force network). 24/7 alerts to the on-call property officer and a tamper-evident continuity record for the FSR Code and court.
notes: c4 Forensic Science Regulator Act 2021 statutory Code; c1 case-loss costs hard to source; c7 crowded fridge-monitor category, niche is evidential audit trail.

title: Prison cell call bells unanswered for 20–40 minutes with no reliable response data
problem: The prison standard is ~5 minutes to answer an emergency cell bell. HMIP repeatedly finds many bells unanswered (e.g. ~40% over 5 min at one inspection), and PPO investigations cite 18–40-minute responses before deaths. Legacy bell systems can't produce data for governors or inspectors.
who_suffers: Prisoners in crisis; landing officers; governors facing HMIP criticism
buyer: Governor / Head of Safer Custody (or private prison director)
industry: UK prisons with legacy hard-wired cell call systems
current_workaround: Manual spot audits of bell response, legacy panel logs that are hard to export, staff observation
sensor_concept: Clip-on optical/current sensors on landing indicator lamps or bell circuits per landing panel timestamp each activation and cancel. LoRaWAN gateway. Response-time dashboard by wing and shift, plus breach alerts to the orderly officer.
notes: c2 daily events; c4/c10 HMIP + PPO evidence; c1 weak (no direct £ per incident) and c5 public procurement — expect lower scores.

title: Prison wing heating failures in winter: cold cells, complaints and FM contract deductions
problem: Ageing prison heating plant fails in winter, and wings sit cold for days. HMIP and IMBs report cold cells, and prisoner complaints and legal claims follow. FM and PFI contracts carry availability deductions and disputes over when the failure started and was fixed (~£k per incident).
who_suffers: Prisoners; residential staff; FM contract managers
buyer: FM Contract Manager / Head of Estates at the prison or PFI operator
industry: UK Victorian and PFI prisons with central boiler/heat distribution
current_workaround: Prisoner and staff complaints, FM helpdesk tickets, occasional manual thermometer readings, BMS where it exists (often not)
sensor_concept: Landing/wing ambient temperature sensors plus flow/return pipe clamps at heating substations. LoRaWAN private gateway. Heating-failure alerts before complaints arrive, and a time-stamped record for performance-deduction disputes.
notes: c2 seasonal recurring; c3 FM callouts; c6 FM contractor on site; c4 weaker (contract terms, not statute).

title: Void commercial buildings: the insurer's 7-day inspection condition is missed and the claim is refused
problem: Unoccupancy clauses typically require inspections within 14 days and then at least every 7 days, recorded, plus water off, drained and the like. Key holders charge ~£25–£60 per visit. Missed or unrecorded visits let squatters, water damage or arson claims (~£10k–£100k+) be repudiated, and records are now central to vacant-pub claims.
who_suffers: Asset managers, LPA receivers, landlords; key-holding firms
buyer: Property/Asset Manager at a commercial landlord or LPA receiver, buying via a key-holding or void-management firm
industry: UK vacant commercial property (shops, pubs, offices, industrial units)
current_workaround: Weekly key-holder or patrol visits with paper/app reports; some void firms fit their own alarms (VPS, Clearway, Orbis)
sensor_concept: Cellular hub with door contacts, PIR, leak, temperature, smoke and mains-power sensors. A daily automated 'virtual inspection' log formatted for insurer evidence, triggered visits on alerts, and fewer routine patrols.
notes: c4 insurer conditions + refused claims; c2 weekly mandated visits; c3 paid key-holder visits; c6 key-holding/void firms and unoccupied-property insurers/brokers.

title: Executors of empty probate homes can't prove the insurer's inspection and drain-down conditions
problem: A deceased person's home sits empty for 6–18 months during probate. Unoccupied-home insurers require weekly/fortnightly inspections and water off/drained (or heating at a minimum temperature) in winter. Executors and solicitors live far away, so a burst pipe claim (~£10–30k+) is declined and the estate or solicitor bears it.
who_suffers: Beneficiaries; executors; private-client solicitors (liability)
buyer: Private Client/Probate Partner at a solicitors' firm or a professional estate administrator
industry: UK probate and estate administration (unoccupied deceased-estate homes)
current_workaround: Relatives or neighbours visit occasionally, solicitors pay local key-holders, paper notes of visits; specialist unoccupied-home insurance
sensor_concept: Rented cellular kit: flow/pulse sensor on the incoming main (proves water off, detects flow), pipe/room temperature, door and PIR. Weekly evidence pack for the insurer and alerts to a key holder. Rental per estate, ~6–12 months.
notes: c4 insurer conditions; c6 probate solicitors and unoccupied-home insurers/brokers as channel; c9 per-estate rental; distinct buyer from commercial voids.

title: Key-holding firms lose track of client key sets in patrol vans
problem: Key-holding and mobile-patrol firms carry thousands of client key sets in vans and safes. BS 7984-1 (NSI approval) expects coded, secure keys with logged movements. A lost set forces the client to change locks or rekey a master suite (~£500–£10k+), and the contract can be lost.
who_suffers: Patrol officers; operations controllers; clients
buyer: Operations Director at an NSI/SSAIB-approved key-holding and mobile-patrol company
industry: UK key-holding and alarm-response companies
current_workaround: Paper or app key sign-out logs, coded tags, vehicle key safes, periodic key audits for NSI inspection
sensor_concept: BLE tag on each key ring, with gateways in the depot key safe and in each patrol vehicle on cellular. A live key-location register and alerts when a set leaves its vehicle or is not returned by shift end. Exportable audit for NSI inspections.
notes: c4 BS 7984/NSI approval requirements; c2 daily key movements; c5/c6 concentrated trade (NSI member list); c1 needs sourced lock-change costs.

title: Vacant business-park plots occupied by unauthorised encampments over bank-holiday weekends
problem: Vacant yards, development plots and business-park car parks are entered over long weekends. By the time anyone notices, an encampment is established, and clean-up runs ~£2–10k+ per incident plus bailiffs, court costs and new fencing/bollards (~£2k+). Council and business-park records show repeated targeting.
who_suffers: Landlords, business-park managers, neighbouring tenants
buyer: Estates/Asset Manager of a business park or development landowner (also council estates teams)
industry: UK business parks, logistics yards awaiting letting and development land
current_workaround: Concrete blocks, bunds and height barriers, ad-hoc security patrols, CCTV towers on high-risk sites
sensor_concept: Magnetometer or radar vehicle detector at each entrance plus tilt sensors on barriers/bollards (forced entry). LoRaWAN/NB-IoT, battery. Instant alert to key holder or security so they can intervene before pitches are set up.
notes: c1 sourced clean-up costs exist (~£2k–£10k); c2 several times/yr at hotspot sites; c6 void-security firms and barrier installers; c4 weak (no regulation).

title: Temporary fence panels unclipped overnight to steal plant and cable from sites
problem: On out-of-hours construction, utility and event sites, thieves unclip or lift temporary fence panels to take plant, tools and cable. Each theft costs ~£k–£50k, and contract-works insurers' security conditions are breached. CCTV towers cost ~£100s/week and still miss the breach point.
who_suffers: Site managers; contractors; insurers
buyer: Security Manager / Site Manager at a contractor, or a mobile security firm offering it as a service
industry: UK construction sites, utility compounds and event sites using hired temporary fencing
current_workaround: Night patrols, CCTV towers, static guards, padlocked couplers
sensor_concept: Tilt/vibration sensors clipped to fence couplers every few panels, LoRaWAN to a solar gateway with cellular backhaul. Breach alerts with panel location to the ARC/key holder. Hired with the fence.
notes: c1 plant/cable theft costs sourced widely; c6 fence-hire companies and security firms already on site; c7 CCTV towers incumbent; overlaps with construction.

title: Roller shutters left half-up overnight breach the insurance protection warranty
problem: Commercial policies for trade counters, shops and warehouses carry protection warranties: shutters down, alarm set, keys removed. Staff leave a shutter partly up or the alarm unset, and a theft claim (~£k–£50k) is declined for breach of warranty.
who_suffers: Branch managers; business owners; brokers
buyer: Branch/Store Manager or Risk Manager at a multi-branch trade-counter or retail chain
industry: UK trade counters, builders' merchants, multi-branch retailers and small warehouses
current_workaround: Closing checklists, alarm open/close reports from ARC (where monitored), manager phone calls
sensor_concept: Shutter position sensor (tilt/magnet at bottom rail) plus an alarm-set state from a panel output, on a cellular node. Alerts the duty manager if the shutter is not down or the alarm not set by X minutes after closing, with a nightly warranty-compliance log for the broker.
notes: c4 insurer protection warranties; c2 nightly check; c6 shutter maintainers/alarm installers/brokers; c1 needs sourced declined-claim cases.

title: Registered firearms dealers and sporting estates: gun-room and cabinet break-ins
problem: RFDs and shooting estates must meet police firearms security conditions. Thefts of shotguns and rifles from gun rooms lead to certificate reviews, insurer losses (~£k–£50k) and guns entering crime. Prying attacks on cabinets are often missed by the intruder alarm.
who_suffers: Dealers, estate head keepers, certificate holders
buyer: RFD owner or Estate Manager / Head Keeper
industry: UK registered firearms dealers, gunsmiths and sporting estates
current_workaround: Steel cabinets to BS 7558, intruder alarms, police firearms-enquiry-officer inspections, paper dealer registers
sensor_concept: Cabinet door contact plus accelerometer/tilt (prying, cutting, removal) and room PIR on an independent cellular node. Alerts to the owner and ARC, and every opening is logged as an audit trail alongside the dealer's register.
notes: c4 police security conditions/Home Office guidance; c6 shooting insurers (BASC, Countryside Alliance) and cabinet suppliers; c5 small buyers; c2 risk: rare thefts.

title: Repeat false alarms lose a site its police response, and the insurer requires that response
problem: Under NPCC alarm policy, sites with repeated false alarms in a rolling 12 months get police response downgraded or withdrawn. Insurers often require police-response alarms. Each false activation also costs a key-holder callout (~£40–£80), and installers can't find the cause (draughty doors, insects, heating).
who_suffers: Business owners; alarm installers' service teams; key holders
buyer: Service Manager at an NSI/SSAIB alarm installer (recharging the client), or the business owner
industry: UK commercial intruder alarm maintenance (police-response URN sites)
current_workaround: Repeat engineer visits, swapping detectors, masking zones, reading panel logs
sensor_concept: Clip-on 'flight recorder' sensors near suspect detectors (door rattle accelerometer, temperature/airflow, light/humidity), LoRa to a cellular hub. Correlates environmental spikes with ARC alarm timestamps and reports the root cause for each false alarm.
notes: c4 NPCC policy + insurer conditions; c6 alarm installers visit 2×/yr; c8 physics fuzzy (~5); c9 likely short-term diagnostic rental, so weaker.

title: Wall-mounted A/C condensate pump fails and drips onto the rack in a small comms room
problem: Small server and comms rooms are often cooled by a wall or cassette split unit mounted above the racks. The condensate pump fails or the drain blocks, water drips into switches or servers, and a building or school loses network for a day. Kit replacement and downtime cost ~£5–20k.
who_suffers: IT/MSP staff; schools, surgeries, offices losing service
buyer: Facilities Manager (or School Business Manager) via their HVAC maintenance contractor
industry: UK schools, GP surgeries, council and SME office comms/server rooms
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: 6-monthly or annual A/C service including F-gas checks, occasional visual checks; generic room-temperature monitors on the IT network
sensor_concept: Current clamp on the condensate pump, float in the drip tray, leak rope under the unit and room temperature. LoRaWAN/NB-IoT, no customer IT. Alerts to the HVAC contractor and MSP before water reaches the rack, and a service log.
notes: c6 HVAC/F-gas contractors visit 1–4×/yr; c8 cheap, no IT; c7 generic room monitors exist, but niche failure mode and channel are distinct.

title: Duty/standby comms-room A/C: the standby unit never actually takes over
problem: Comms rooms with two split units on a lead-lag controller find out the standby has failed, or the changeover controller is faulty, only when the duty unit trips on a weekend. The room passes ~40°C, switches and servers shut down or are damaged, and outage plus kit costs ~£k–£20k.
who_suffers: IT teams; occupants; facilities manager
buyer: Facilities/Estates Manager at a council, college, hospital trust or multi-academy trust
industry: UK public-sector and SME comms rooms with N+1 DX split cooling
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: Changeover tested at annual or 6-monthly service, if at all; IT-network temperature alerts that fail when the network fails
sensor_concept: CT clamps on both indoor/outdoor units plus supply-air and room temperature. LoRaWAN. Proves weekly duty rotation, alerts when the duty unit is off and the standby didn't start, and gives a runtime report for the HVAC contractor.
notes: c6 HVAC contractors; c2 weekly rotation proof; c3 contractor visits; c4 weak (no regulation), c1 needs sourced outage costs.

title: Server-room gas-suppression cylinders leak agent between 6-monthly services
problem: FM-200, Novec or inert-gas suppression cylinders slowly lose agent. BS EN 15004 / ISO 14520 require 6-monthly checks of contents, and a low system may not reach design concentration in a fire. Recharging FM-200 is costly and scarce under the HFC phase-down (~£k–£10k+), and F-gas rules require leak checks for HFC systems.
who_suffers: Data-centre/facilities managers; suppression service firms
buyer: Facilities Manager of a server room, or a fire-suppression service company bundling it
industry: UK/EU server rooms, comms rooms and archive rooms with clean-agent suppression
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: 6-monthly service visit weighing cylinders or reading liquid-level indicators; gauge with low-pressure switch on some systems
sensor_concept: Strain-gauge load cell under each cylinder (or a temperature-compensated pressure transducer on the gauge port). LoRaWAN/NB-IoT. Continuous agent-quantity trend, leak alerts and an F-gas/BS EN 15004 records export for the service contractor.
notes: c4 BS EN 15004 + F-gas regs; c6 suppression service companies visit 2×/yr; c1 refill costs sourceable; c8 risk: modifying pressure ports needs care.

title: Standby generator won't start at a small data centre: flat start battery or water in the diesel
problem: At small colocation sites, telephone exchanges in private hands and comms hubs, the standby generator fails to start on mains loss. Causes are a flat starter battery, a failed block heater, or water/diesel bug in a tank that sat for years. The outage breaches SLAs (~£k–£100k+ in credits/claims).
who_suffers: Colo/hosting operators; their customers
buyer: Facilities/Operations Manager at a regional colocation or hosting provider
industry: UK/EU small and regional data centres and comms hubs with diesel standby sets
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: Monthly off-load test runs, quarterly generator service contracts, annual fuel testing/polishing by fuel-care firms
sensor_concept: Starter battery voltage, block-heater temperature, tank level, and a capacitive water-in-fuel probe at the tank bottom. NB-IoT. Alerts to the generator service contractor, an auto monthly test log and fuel-polishing triggers.
notes: c6 generator service and fuel-polishing firms visit; c2 monthly tests; c7 DSE controller telemetry exists for newer sets, gap is fuel quality and older sets.

title: UPS VRLA batteries cooking in hot comms cupboards fail at the first power cut
problem: VRLA battery life roughly halves for each ~10°C above 25°C. UPSs in hot comms cupboards and risers lose their batteries in 1–2 years instead of 4–5, then fail at the first power cut. Replacement costs ~£1–10k plus unplanned outage.
who_suffers: IT and facilities teams; users losing service
buyer: Facilities Manager or the UPS maintenance contractor (bundled service)
industry: UK branch offices, schools, retail head offices and industrial sites with small/mid UPSs
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: Annual UPS maintenance visit with battery impedance test, scheduled battery swaps by age
sensor_concept: Thermistor on the battery string and string voltage/float current via a clamp-on sensor, plus ambient temperature. LoRaWAN, no IT. Predicted end-of-life, hot-cupboard alerts and an annual battery-health report for the UPS contractor.
notes: c6 UPS maintenance contractors visit annually; c3 paid battery swaps; c4 weak; c1 needs sourced outage costs.

title: EU data centres over 500 kW must report PUE/energy/water each year but have no sub-metering
problem: EU Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791 Art. 12 and Delegated Reg 2024/1364 require data centres ≥500 kW IT load to report energy, PUE, water use and waste heat annually. Mid-size enterprise, university and hospital server rooms lack sub-metering and estimate. National penalties apply, e.g. Germany's EnEfG fines up to ~€100k.
who_suffers: Data-centre/energy managers compiling reports
buyer: Energy Manager or Data Centre Facilities Manager at an enterprise/university/hospital
industry: EU (esp. DE, NL, IE, FR) enterprise and public-sector data centres in the 500 kW–2 MW band
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: Manual meter readings, spreadsheets, consultant-led estimates once a year
sensor_concept: Split-core CT clamps with LoRaWAN on UPS input/output and cooling plant distribution boards, a pulse reader on water meters, and a cellular gateway. Monthly KPI dashboard and auto-generated EED reporting dataset.
notes: c4 named EU regulation with penalties; c9 annual statutory reporting; c5 risk: IT-adjacent buyer; c8 CT install needs an electrician.

title: Builders' dust gets into live server rooms during refurbishment works
problem: Drilling, chasing and cutting next to or inside a live server room during refurbishments lets dust into server intakes. It clogs filters and causes failures or hot spots. Client-contractor disputes and claims run ~£k–£100k, and DC operators demand dust control in method statements.
who_suffers: Client IT/DC managers; fit-out contractors
buyer: Project Manager at a fit-out/M&E contractor, or the client's DC Manager specifying it
industry: UK office/data-room fit-out and refurbishment near live IT spaces
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: Dust sheets, temporary partitions, negative pressure units, visual checks, post-works deep clean (~£k)
sensor_concept: Laser particulate sensor (PM1/2.5/10), door differential pressure and temperature on battery/mains nodes, rented per project with cellular backhaul. Live alerts to site supervisor and a compliance report proving dust control.
notes: c3 paid cleans/partitions; c9 per-project rental; c6 fit-out contractors; c4 weak (contract method statements only).

title: ISO 27001 auditors flag unmonitored comms cupboards in branch offices
problem: ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.4 requires premises to be continuously monitored for unauthorised physical access. Branch comms cupboards and racks opened by cleaners or contractors leave no record, and certification audits raise non-conformities. Delays risk lost tenders that require certification (~£k–£100k contracts).
who_suffers: ISMS managers; MSPs maintaining branch sites
buyer: Information Security/ISMS Manager (or MSP selling managed compliance)
industry: UK multi-branch SMEs (recruitment, legal, logistics) holding ISO 27001
sector: Data centres, server rooms & comms rooms
current_workaround: Locks and key logs, CCTV where it exists, manual access sheets on cupboard doors
sensor_concept: Rack/cupboard door contact plus vibration/tamper and temperature. LoRaWAN/NB-IoT, independent of the corporate network. Physical-access event log exported for audit, with alerts out of hours.
notes: c4 named standard clause; c6 MSPs/ISO consultants; c5 −2 risk because buyer is IT; c1 weak.
